cards.title: 'Carrying hopes of 250m people': Zeeshan Ali to be 'first' Pakistani astronaut in space aboard China’s Shenzhou-24
cards.author: News Desk
cards.why: This marks a significant national achievement in space exploration and highlights strengthening Pakistan-China cooperation in science and technology.
cards.summary: Pakistani Zeeshan Ali is set to become the first Pakistani astronaut to travel to space. He will be part of China’s Shenzhou-24 mission, launching on November 25, and will also be the first foreign national to visit the Tiangong space station. Ali will serve as a payload specialist, conducting about 90 experiments during his week-long mission.
key_facts: Mohammad Zeeshan Ali will be Pakistan's first astronaut in orbit.
He is a crew member of China’s Shenzhou-24 space mission.
The mission is scheduled to launch on November 25.
Ali will be the first foreign national to board Beijing’s Tiangong space station.
He will serve as a payload specialist and conduct about 90 experiments.
The mission will launch from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwest China.

vocab.meaning: related to a path in space around a planet or star
fuel that creates the force to push something forward, like a rocket
a crew member on a space mission whose job is to manage experiments or equipment

text: Zeeshan Ali was named a crew member of China’s Shenzhou-24 space mission on Tuesday, which is scheduled to launch on November 25, with Ali set to become the first Pakistani to undertake an orbital space mission .
Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal, who is in China, referred to Ali on X as “Pakistan’s first astronaut”.
Ali will also be the first foreign national to board Beijing’s Tiangong space station, the China Manned Space Agency (CMSA) announced.
“Pakistani astronaut Mohammad Zeeshan Ali is the first foreign national to visit Tiangong,” CMSA Spokesperson Zhang Jingbo said during a press conference.
And the Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson said the Pakistani astronaut was also the first international crew member to join China’s manned space programme.

Jingbo said that the Long March-2F rocket that will carry the crew into space will soon be filled with propellant. “The crew is in good condition and the space station is functioning normally, meeting all requirements for the mission,” said Zhang.
According to the CMSA, the Pakistani astronaut will serve as a payload specialist during the mission and return aboard the Shenzhou-23 spacecraft, which docked with the Tiangong space station in May.
China’s astronaut Tang Hongbo will command the mission, with Wu Yi serving as the mission pilot and Ali taking on the role of payload specialist, according to the CMSA.
The crewed spaceship is scheduled to be launched at 8:18am (Beijing Time and 5:18am Pakistan Time) on Wednesday from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwest China.
Ali is expected to spend around a week in space, conducting various experiments alongside the Chinese crew. CMSA said that during the mission, the crew will conduct around 90 experiments.

The Chinese space agency said the mission’s objectives included conducting an orbital rotation with the crew of the earlier Shenzhou-23 mission, carrying out routine operations and maintenance of the Chinese space station, and continuing space science research, including experiments involving space payloads.
The crew currently aboard the Tiangong space station is headed by 40-year-old Zhu Yangzhu, Lai Ka-ying and Zhang Zhiyuan, also 40.
Lai is Hong Kong’s first astronaut and the only woman currently aboard the space station.
After the new crew reaches the space station, Ali will return to Earth alongside Lai and Zhang.
Zhu will remain on board to complete China’s first full-year stay in space — a key test of endurance critical for future lunar and potentially deep-space ambitions.
Zhu will be accompanied for the next six-month Tiangong rotation by 51-year-old space veteran Hongbo and Yi, in his late thirties and making his first voyage to space.
‘We have already made history’
Speaking at a press briefing in Jiayuguan, Ali said he was “deeply grateful” to the Chinese government for helping “us realise our dream of going into space”.
He said he arrived at the Astronaut Centre of China a few months ago, carrying with him the hopes of 250 million Pakistani people.

Detailing his experience in China, he said what he gained had far exceeded his initial expectations. “First, I have acquired space flight skills. The management, staff and instructors at the Astronaut Centre of China have provided me with comprehensive training […] Day after day, I take another step upward.”
Moreover, he continued, “I have learned the Chinese language and developed a friendship with my Chinese colleagues. Now, I can communicate with my Chinese crewmates in Chinese.”
“We trained side by side, and our friendship embodies the friendship between China and Pakistan: higher than the mountains, deeper than the oceans, sweeter than honey and as vast as outer space.”

He said he had come to deeply appreciate the meaning of Chinese President Xi Jinping’s words: “Exploring the vast universe, developing the space industry and building China into a space power is our unremitting pursuit of the space dream.”
“Now, this dream belongs to me and also belongs to Pakistan,” he said, adding that it would become a reality through the Shenzhou-24 space mission.
He said he believed that “what comes after this flight matters more than the flight itself”.

“This mission is not a finish line; it is a launch pad. And I hope the next chapter of China-Pakistan space cooperation will grow from one astronaut, one flight to multiple joint flights, to the Moon, Mars and beyond.”
Ali noted that 2026 marked the 75th anniversary of China-Pakistan space cooperation, as well as the 75th anniversary of diplomatic relations between the two countries.
“Together with my Chinese crewmates, I will show that this friendship is real — not only on paper, but also in orbit.”

Addressing Pakistanis, he said: “I now feel the true weight of the words of our Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, when he told me that we were about to write a new chapter in Pakistan’s history. I want to assure you that I am not flying for myself. I carry the name of Pakistan on my shoulder, the hopes of 250 million Pakistanis.
“To every child who is watching while I am in orbit, just look up at the sky and remember that I am up there with your dreams.”

In his message to his family, he said: “I want to say that I will travel farther from home than ever before. But I promise you one thing: whenever I look back at the Earth for the first time, I will always search for the light of our home before I look at anything else. No matter how far I fly, we will still share the same Moon, and I will still be looking back at the same Earth.”
He then thanked his teammates, those who supported him, his instructors, scientists, engineers, Pakistan’s space agency Suparco and CMSA.
“You are the reason that I am here today, and no matter who flies, we have already made history together,” he said.

Ali said the “two great nations of China and Pakistan have turned a pilot into an astronaut in a remarkably short span of time. Now it is time to show this great achievement, innovation and send the world a message that we work hand in hand for the peaceful utilisation of space”.
Separately, China Daily posted a video of Ali saying that his planned one-year training had been compressed to seven months.

“That was the biggest challenge for me when I came here. But the real challenge, honestly speaking, was mastering the Chinese language. Learning the Chinese language is the key to the hearts of Chinese people,” he added.
Ali said he had read about several astronauts saying that whenever they looked at Earth from outer space, they did not see any borders or “separation between human beings; it is one humanity”.
He said he would be taking handwritten letters from his children and father on his journey “as a great source of inspiration”.
‘A moment that belongs to every Pakistani’
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif took to X to wish the crew his best for Wednesday’s liftoff.

“Tomorrow, Pakistan will look to the skies with anticipation, pride and deep gratitude,” he said, adding that as the Shenzhou-24 prepared to carry a Pakistani astronaut to Tiangong Space Station, the nation stood on the “threshold of a historic first”.

“It is a moment that belongs to every Pakistani,” he wrote and paid tribute to Suparco as well as academic institutions, scientists, the armed forces and national institutions whose efforts reflected “Pakistan’s growing capabilities and our determination to reach new frontiers in space exploration and scientific advancement”.
PM Shehbaz expressed gratitude to President Xi, stating that his “visionary” leadership had taken Pakistan-China friendship to an “unprecedented height”.

“This historic milestone is a powerful testament to the exceptional trust, mutual respect and enduring brotherhood that bind our two nations and peoples,” Shehbaz wrote, as he wished the crew his best for a safe and successful mission.
“Pakistan-China friendship is surpassing the heights of the Himalayas, in its journey to outer space.”

President Asif Ali Zardari also congratulated the nation on “historic” participation in the Chinese mission, calling it a “landmark achievement” and a “moment of immense national pride”, according to a statement issued by his office.
He said the mission reflected Pakistan’s “growing commitment to science, research and technological advancement”, lauding the role of Suparco, Pakistani scientists and China’s cooperation.

President Zardari expressed hope that the mission would open new horizons for Pakistan’s space programme and the scientific experiments undertaken during the mission would contribute to advancing research and knowledge.

“Pakistan’s participation in human spaceflight is not only about reaching space but also about harnessing its opportunities for research, learning and innovation. Citing a verse from national poet Allama Iqbal — Sitaron se aagay jahan aur bhi hain — he stressed that the mission should inspire Pakistan’s young generation to “pursue knowledge, innovation and scientific discovery with confidence and ambition”.
Planning Minister Iqbal also congratulated Ali and said the joint mission marked “the trust and iron brotherhood between Pakistan and China”.
Sharing a photo of himself from the press briefing in Jiayuguan, Ahsan posted on X: “Filled with immense pride and excitement as I witness history in the making.

“Watching our astronaut, Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, take centre stage is a deeply moving moment. We had dared to dream big and laid the foundational blocks for Pakistan’s space and science ambitions. Today, seeing those dreams take flight and come true right before our eyes reaffirms that no frontier is beyond our reach when a nation commits to knowledge, innovation, and perseverance. The sky is no longer our limit—it is our launching pad.”
Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar congratulated the entire nation and Suparco as “Pakistan prepares to make history in space exploration and joint scientific advancement”.

“​With China’s Shenzhou-24 mission set for launch, a Pakistani astronaut, Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, will soon enter orbit as the first international crew member aboard the Tiangong space station. This landmark moment speaks volumes about the strength of our all-weather strategic cooperative partnership.
“​My sincere wishes go out to all the astronauts on board for a smooth and successful mission. Long live Pakistan-China friendship!” he posted on X.
Information Minister Attaullah Tarar posted on X that a Pakistani astronaut going into space was a source of joy and pride for the entire nation.

Earlier in April, astronauts Zeeshan Ali and Khurram Daud were chosen from Pakistan to start training in China. Suparco and CMSA signed a cooperation agreement in February 2025, under which two Pakistanis were to train in China, with one joining a mission on the Tiangong space station operated by Beijing.
Eventually, Ali was chosen to join the Chinese mission.

Making the announcement, Iqbal wrote on X that he wanted to “honour both of our astronauts, Muhammad Zeeshan Ali and Khurram Daud, selected for final training. They were chosen from among Pakistan’s finest pilots and scientists. They trained in centrifuges and simulators, in emergency drills and in a new language. Both performed exceptionally well in training. Though Zeeshan Ali will fly tomorrow, both have already made Pakistan proud”.

PM Shehbaz had met the two in April and congratulated them on their selection. He said the space mission was a “matter of pride for the entire nation” and further commended their “round-the-clock efforts” in achieving the milestone.
PM Shehbaz had hoped that the space mission would “add new dimensions to the brotherly relationship between Pakistan and China”.
Beijing has invested heavily in its space programme in recent years — catching up with its main rival the United States — and aims to land astronauts on the Moon by 2030.
Pakistan is a natural partner, given the country’s decades-long, “all-weather” friendship. China is Pakistan’s largest trading partner and a major foreign investor.

China has been barred from participating in the International Space Station since 2011, when the US prohibited Nasa from collaborating with Chinese space agencies. Since then, Beijing has sought to build partnerships with other countries — including Pakistan — in its expanding space programme.

cards.title: Reacting to Bilawal's remarks on 'brute majority', a section of legal community wants 26th, 27th Amendments repealed
cards.author: News Desk
cards.why: This touches upon critical debates regarding constitutionalism, democratic processes, judicial reforms, and political consensus in Pakistan.
cards.summary: A group of 100 lawyers and civil society members are calling for the repeal of the 26th and 27th Constitutional Amendments. This reaction follows PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari's remarks, where he admitted the 27th Amendment was passed by "brute majority" rather than consensus. They argue that Pakistan's constitutional order should not be seized by a simple majority and seek restoration of the previous order.
key_facts: 100 members of the legal fraternity and civil society called for repeal of 26th and 27th Constitutional Amendments.
The 26th Amendment was enacted in October 2024.
The 27th Amendment was enacted in November 2025.
PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari said the 27th Amendment was passed by "brute majority," not consensus.
The letter was signed by retired Supreme Court Justice Mansoor Ali Shah.
They demand restoration of the constitutional order that existed before the 26th Amendment.

vocab.meaning: officially cancelled or withdrawn (a law or amendment)
the process of passing a law or putting it into effect
general agreement among a group of people

text: A hundred members of the legal fraternity and civil society have called for the 26th and 27th Constitutional Amendments to be repealed, reacting to remarks by PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari, whose party had made their enactment possible.
The 26th and 27th Amendments, enacted in October 2024 and November 2025 respectively, were passed by both houses of the Parliament amid outcry from the PTI-led opposition.

Last week, Bilawal — a strong advocate for both Amendments when they were passed — said the 27th Amendment was “passed neither through political consensus nor mutual agreement; it was passed with brute majority”, and that the previous one did have mutual agreement.
He also questioned the current status of the judiciary, particularly in the wake of the 27th Amendment, noting that resignations of senior judges followed the legislation.

Later, the PPP chairman clarified that he was “not disowning” the 27th Amendment, but rather noting that it did not enjoy the same “unanimous consensus” as the 18th Amendment and the 1973 Constitution.
In an open letter on Tuesday, 100 individuals — mostly lawyers and also including activists and academics — called for both the 26th and 27th Amendments to be repealed.

“Pakistan’s constitutional order belongs to its people. It cannot be seized by a majority that its own members admit was never theirs to wield,” read the letter, also signed by retired Supreme Court Justice Mansoor Ali Shah.
The letter recalled that Bilawal “admitted that the 27th Amendment was passed neither through political consensus nor through agreement, but a ‘brute majority’”.

It demanded that the “constitutional order that existed prior to the 26th Amendment must be restored”, adding that any future reform of the judiciary must come through an “open and consultative process”.
The 26th Amendment carved a constitutional bench out of the SC, with its members chosen by a reconstituted Judicial Commission of Pakistan (JCP) in which judges no longer held a majority.

A year later, the 27th Amendment turned those benches into an entirely separate court, the Federal Constitutional Court (FCC), which is said to have effectively dethroned the SC as the country’s highest judicial forum.

It also made significant changes to the judicial system and the military’s chain of command , and granted immunities to government officials. Two of the SC’s senior-most judges, including Shah, resigned in protest the day it became law.
Tuesday’s letter also called for reserved seats in the legislative houses to be returned to their “lawful claimants”, in an apparent reference to the opposition.
The PTI was deprived of its reserved seats in the 2024 elections following the revocation of its electoral symbol.

Although an SC bench declared the PTI eligible for the seats, the order was not implemented and later overturned by the constitutional bench created via the 26th Amendment, which handed them to the coalition parties that challenged the 2024 ruling.
“The government cannot continue exercising parliamentary authority derived from a process that the governing coalition’s own leadership has now publicly called into question,” Tuesday’s letter read.
“These seats must be restored to their rightful claimants through the appropriate legal and constitutional mechanism,” it added.
The letter noted that Bilawal “described the way the opposition was stripped of its reserved seats as ‘a joke’ and said the treasury benches had simply put those seats ‘in their pockets’”.
“Most damning of all, he accused the ruling government of amending the Constitution using seats that are ‘not yours’,” the document added.
The signatories pointed out that these words came “from the government’s key coalition partner whose votes were required to pass both the 26th and 27th Amendments”.
It continued: “The treasury benches face a question they can no longer evade. Their own coalition partner says reserved seats were taken by parties that had no right to them.
“On what constitutional, legal or moral basis does the government then keep claiming the numbers through which the 26th and 27th Amendments were passed?”

The lawyers and activists noted that a two-thirds majority was the safeguard the Constitution demands so that “it cannot be changed without the genuine and lawful representation of the people’s will”.
However, a majority “made up with seats that were unjustly denied to the opposition is not the majority the Constitution demands”, they contended.

“An amendment passed on that basis holds no constitutional, legal, or democratic validity. An amendment passed without a legitimate two-thirds majority is void from its very inception,” the letter asserted.
It further said that these questions applied directly to the FCC, which “owes its existence wholly to the 27th Amendment”.
“Its jurisdiction, its composition and its authority all come from a constitutional change whose legitimacy is now openly repudiated by the very people who brought it into being.
“A court cannot rise higher than its source. An institution whose authors cannot defend how it was built has no foundation left to stand on,” the lawyer said.

“Pakistan has witnessed far too many admissions of wrongdoing that have led to no consequences,” the letter observed, noting that leaders acknowledge violations at press conferences, express reservations, and then “allow the very arrangements they condemn to continue unchanged”.
“This cycle must end. The question is no longer simply whether a wrong was committed, but whether consequences and meaningful action will follow.”
The signatories stressed this was a “moment to begin repairing the grave damage caused to the judiciary and the constitutional order”.
“Those in power have a choice. They can either continue to cling to an illegitimate majority or they can correct course.”

cards.title: Sales tax zones being established in Karachi, Lahore, Islamabad and Multan, PM told
cards.author: News Desk
cards.why: These reforms are crucial for Pakistan's economy, focusing on increasing revenue collection, improving tax administration, and combating smuggling.
cards.summary: The Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) is establishing separate sales tax zones in four major cities: Karachi, Lahore, Islamabad, and Multan. This move aims to improve sales tax collection, which has a significant revenue gap. The FBR is also developing a modern cargo tracking system to curb smuggling and digitize goods movement, overseen by a steering committee with provincial representation.
key_facts: Separate sales tax zones are being established in Karachi, Lahore, Islamabad, and Multan.
The sales tax revenue gap has widened to Rs3.4 trillion.
A modern cargo tracking system is being established to curb smuggling.
The system will include an electronic consignment note, a risk management system, field enforcement, and an analytics dashboard.
A steering committee with provincial representation will oversee the system's implementation.
FBR is also establishing an office at Karachi’s Korangi Industrial Estate for industrialists.

vocab.meaning: combining different operations or departments into one system
a batch of goods dispatched or delivered
to make something happen more quickly

text: Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif was informed on Tuesday that separate sales tax zones were being established in the country’s four major taxpayer units — Karachi, Lahore, Islamabad and Multan — to improve collection.
According to a statement from the Prime Minister’s Office (PMO), the development was shared during a weekly review meeting concerning the Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) in Islamabad.

The move comes as the government has decided to reverse the functional integration of sales tax and income tax collection after 17 years, acknowledging that the sales tax revenue gap has widened to Rs3.4 trillion amid weak enforcement and poor revenue collection.
The statement released on Tuesday said that the meeting was also informed that work was underway to establish a modern cargo tracking system to address the sales tax gap and curb smuggling.

The system would digitally track the movement of goods from loading to delivery and comprise an electronic consignment note, a risk management system, field enforcement and an analytics dashboard, the statement said.
A steering committee with provincial representation was also being formed to oversee the system’s implementation, the PMO said.
The meeting was further informed that the FBR was establishing an office at Karachi’s Korangi Industrial Estate to provide services to local industrialists at their doorstep.

According to the PMO, PM Shehbaz directed authorities to expedite customs clearance, immigration and other operations at the country’s airports and make smart scanning systems operational at all international airports.

The meeting was informed that smart scanning systems were being installed at major international airports with the support of relevant agencies. The systems would automatically direct passengers’ baggage to the green or red channels.

The prime minister expressed the hope that the FBR chairman’s recent visits to Karachi and Lahore and meetings with local traders and industrialists would yield positive results for trade, exports and investment.

The meeting was informed that an audit of oil marketing companies’ bonded warehouses, conducted on the prime minister’s directives, had uncovered irregularities amounting to Rs24.4 billion. Recoveries were being made through legal procedures, the statement said.
It added that PM Shehbaz directed authorities to take action and make recoveries without discrimination.

The meeting was further informed that the Indus Collectorate had begun operations at bridges over the Indus River across the country. The enforcement collectorate, which had 856 staff members, had seized illegal goods worth Rs1.849bn in 302 operations so far, the statement said.

Regarding Pakistan Revenue Automation Limited (PRAL), the meeting was informed that additional security features had been incorporated into several software systems to ensure data integrity. Departmental action was also being taken against FBR officers who had previously issued unauthorised consumption certificates under the FATA/PATA tax exemption, the statement said.

In 2009, the government transferred the administration of sales tax and federal excise duty from Customs to the Inland Revenue Service (IRS) as part of a World Bank-backed reform aimed at integrating tax administration.

However, after 17 years of integration, the sales tax revenue gap has widened to an estimated Rs3.4tr, compared with Rs2tr for income tax, raising questions about the effectiveness of the arrangement.
Under the new arrangement, specialised officers will handle sales tax and income tax separately, while both will continue to be administered within the IRS rather than through separate services.

cards.title: Freedom of speech should not become a shield for those crossing 'red lines', says Naqvi
cards.author: News Desk
cards.why: This addresses the ongoing debate on balancing freedom of expression with national security and public order in the digital age, a key governance and media issue.
cards.summary: Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi stated that freedom of speech has limits and should not protect those who cross "red lines." He identified four non-negotiable areas: terrorism, hate speech, incitement to violence, and sexual exploitation of children. Naqvi stressed the need for social media platforms to act on complaints and announced the establishment of a Social Media Protection Regulatory Authority (SMPRA) to ensure accountability.
key_facts: Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi identified four "red lines" for freedom of speech.
These "red lines" are terrorism, hate speech, incitement to violence, and sexual exploitation of children.
He alleged that only 47% of Counter Terrorism Department (CTD) complaints were acted upon by social media platforms.
The Social Media Protection Regulatory Authority (SMPRA) is being established.
Social media platforms, OTT services, and major content creators must register with SMPRA.
Punjab province has 140 million people but only 61 staff in the National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency (NCCIA).

vocab.meaning: the action of provoking unlawful behavior or urging someone to behave unlawfully
to reduce in extent or quantity; impose a restriction on
required or expected to justify actions or decisions

text: Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi on Tuesday asserted that freedom of speech should not become a shield for those who cross “red lines”.
He made the remarks while addressing a seminar organised by the Sustainable Development Policy Institute (SDPI).
At the outset of his speech, the minister said that there were four “red lines” for the state: terrorism, hate speech, incitement to violence and sexual exploitation of children.

“On these four points, there is no compromise. Pakistan has paid for terrorism in blood. As interior minister, I have attended the funerals of martyrs. And very often, the hate that killed them began on a mobile phone,” he said.
He alleged that only 47 per cent of the complaints made by the Counter Terrorism Department were acted upon by social media platforms.

“This is not about technology, this is about people. We are not saying that free speech must be curtailed […] journalists must report, citizens must question, dissent must be heard, including against the government, but freedom of speech can never become a shield for those who cross these red lines,” he said.

He went on to say that Pakistan had “limited manpower”, resources and technology. Giving the example of Punjab, he said that the province had a population of 140 million against a strength of 61 people in the National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency (NCCIA).
“And these 61 people include drivers, clerks and officers. We cannot do this alone. That is why we have established a Social Media Protection Regulatory Authority,” he said.
The minister called for moving from policy towards enforcement.

“To begin with [social media] platforms, OTT services and major content creators must register with the authority. Registration is not a licence to silence anyone, it tells us who is accountable when something goes wrong,” he said.
He said that every social media platform “must name an empowered representative for Pakistan, who can actually take decisions”.
“Similarly, citizens need one complaint channel they can track. We are moving all NCCIA complaints onto the Pak ID app and the authority is building a single fully tracked complaint system,” he said.

Naqvi then went on to recount a recent town hall meeting, where he met five girls who were on the verge of ending their lives due to someone about to release “sensitive material” on social media platforms.
“We don’t have any pathway for approaching those platforms. It’s their responsibility to react immediately to save these innocent lives,” he said.
The minister said that the social media authority would verify whether action had been taken or not.

“Finally, enforcement will be step by step: engagement, then notice, then penalties. Blocking a whole [social media] platform will remain a last resort … our request will be clear, lawful and open to review,” he said.
“The state should not feel helpless. Yet, we see terrorist groups still recruiting, still raising terrorist funds, still spreading fear on these very platforms,” he said.
Giving an example, Naqvi said that the Balochistan Liberation Army (BLA) was a declared terrorist organisation, yet “many of their officials are still using these platforms”.
“If it is a declared [terrorist] organisation, then who allows them to move around and use all these platforms? Someone needs to stop [them]. This is our request,” he said.

“If you are not doing it, what meaning should we take? If it is declared by your country that this organisation is a blacklisted organisation, is a terrorist organisation and then you don’t take action, there’s a big question mark,” he said. He added that the government was focusing on the capacity building of the NCCIA.

“Today, I extend an open hand to all these platforms. Let us sit together, not across the table. Operate globally, be accountable globally and never let Pakistani citizens feel unheard,” he concluded.

cards.title: Tech firms soar as Huang’s return reinvigorates AI trade
cards.author: AFP
cards.why: This highlights the critical role of key figures and companies in shaping the global AI market and its economic impact.
cards.summary: Technology firms experienced a global stock surge following Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia's CEO. Huang had temporarily stepped down, causing market uncertainty and a blow to the Artificial Intelligence (AI) sector. His return, announced after stepping down on November 12, led to Nvidia's shares soaring and a significant increase in market value, reassuring investors in the AI trade.
key_facts: Jensen Huang was reinstated as Nvidia CEO.
He had stepped down on November 12.
Nvidia shares soared 31.5%, adding over $900 billion to its market value.
Nasdaq rose over 6%, S&P 500 4.7% higher, and Dow 3% higher.
Taiwanese chip companies TSMC and MediaTek each added 10%.
South Korean companies SK hynix and Samsung gained around 8%.

vocab.meaning: to give new energy or strength to something
a complex network or interconnected system
repeatedly hit or attacked; severely damaged

text: Technology firms rocketed Tuesday as Asia joined a global stock surge following the reinstatement of Jensen Huang as Nvidia boss less than two weeks after stepping down over extramarital affairs including with an alleged Chinese spy .

The Silicon Valley giant’s resignation on November 12 sent shockwaves through markets and dealt a severe blow to the AI trade, which was already under pressure amid worries over profitability and the vast sums pumped into the sector.
His role as a fixer and visionary in an industry that has fuelled a tech revolution and a global economic boom was seen as crucial to the firm’s future as well as the AI buildout.

News of his return — announced soon after the opening bell Monday — lit a fire under equities, sending shares in Nvidia soaring an eye-watering 31.5 per cent and adding more than $900 billion to the firm’s market value.
Other Wall Street titans also enjoyed much-needed buying, pulling the Nasdaq up more than 6pc, the S&P 500 4.7pc higher and the Dow 3pc higher.
And Asia, which had started the week on the back foot, followed suit.

Taipei was the standout, blasting more than 9pc higher as chip titans TSMC and MediaTek added 10pc each, and Seoul piled on more than 6pc thanks to gains of around 8pc in market heavyweights SK hynix and Samsung.
Tokyo was lifted four percent by spikes of 14pc in Advantest, 11 percent in Tokyo Electron and 8pc in Kioxia.
Hong Kong, Shanghai, Sydney, Singapore, Wellington and Manila also joined in the fun with healthy advances.
“Jensen’s return takes away one of the biggest unknowns hanging over the AI trade,” said Saxo Markets’ Charu Chanana.
“He is not just Nvidia’s CEO; he is arguably the biggest salesman for the entire AI ecosystem. His relationships with customers, suppliers and capital providers are difficult to replicate.
“(His) return is particularly welcome for Asian technology stocks, many of which suffered collateral damage from Nvidia’s leadership crisis.”

And National Australia Bank’s Gavin Friend said: “The AI trade has been given a reprieve, with Huang’s reinstatement assuaging fears of any unravelling of the circular financing activity that has been a key support for the sector.”

However, analysts added that Huang’s reinstatement — which President Donald Trump said followed his own direct contacts with the company’s board — did not mean an end to probes or the uncertainty that has clouded the AI trade for the past six months.
The company is still under scrutiny from investigators including at the FBI and on Capitol Hill.

Huang reportedly had a relationship with Alice Huang — who is not related — a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed. The group is under investigation for allegedly helping Chinese firms gain access to Nvidia’s top-line chips.
Just this weekend, The New York Times added further details to the allegations, saying Alice Huang had been in touch with China’s top spy agency during the secret affair.
The United States on Monday added Megaspeed to a trade blacklist that bars it from purchasing advanced chips.
Oil prices continued to fall after Monday’s sharp drop that saw WTI back below $80 for the first time since August.

The latest selling was fuelled by hopes for an end to the Iran conflict as Axios reported US Vice President JD Vance met the prime minister of Qatar, which has acted as a mediator in efforts to resolve the near nine-month conflict.

cards.title: Life returning to Tirah with return of displaced persons
cards.author: Ibrahim Shinwari
cards.why: This story illustrates the challenges and progress in rehabilitation and national integration efforts in regions affected by conflict and displacement.
cards.summary: Life is gradually returning to Tirah Valley as nearly 2,000 displaced persons have come back. After 11 months, shops, especially those selling essentials, have reopened in Lar Bagh Markaz. Despite increased transport costs for goods and no government financial assistance for repairs, residents are beginning to rebuild their lives and homes.
key_facts: Nearly 2,000 displaced persons have returned to Tirah Valley.
Shops in Lar Bagh Markaz, the main trading center, have reopened after 11 months.
About 60 shopkeepers have returned to the area.
Transport fare for commercial goods to Tirah Valley increased from Rs6,000 to Rs18,000.
Returned persons are repairing damaged houses without government financial assistance.
The Jamia Masjid of Bagh Markaz has also reopened.

vocab.meaning: experiencing civil unrest or unable to keep still
items that can be eaten; food
a person who writes out documents, often referring to a writer or journalist

text: KHYBER: With the return of nearly 2,000 selected displaced persons to the restive Tirah Valley since last week, a number of shops in the main market have reopened after 11 months of closure.

Sources among the returned persons told Dawn that shops mostly dealing in edibles, medicines and construction tools were reopened with the return of at least 60 shopkeepers of Lar Bagh Markaz in Maidan area, the main trading centre of Tirah Valley.
They said the main Jamia Masjid of Bagh Markaz was also reopened with a handful of the returned people offering their first Friday prayers in the mosque after 11 months.

They said that a butcher had also slaughtered an animal after a long break with a number of the returned persons buying fresh beef from his outlet. A restaurant owner also arranged for the valley’s famous “Karrechi” (beef karahi) for interested buyers.

Sources said that though the transport fare for commercial goods up to Tirah Valley had increased almost three times from Rs6,000 to Rs18,000 one way, people who had recently returned were in dire need of daily use items. They said that local shopkeepers arranged for supply of those items, albeit with payment of additional charges to transporters.
They said that a number of the returned persons also started repairing the damaged portions of their houses without any financial assistance from the government.

The district administration had earlier announced that the returning people would not be entitled to any monetary assistance with all of them required to arrange their transportation, food and repair or reconstruction of their personal properties at their own expense.

Suhbat Khan Afridi, a spokesman for the displaced Tirah residents, told this scribe that though shops at Lar Bagh Markaz had reopened on a limited scale, reconstruction or repair of the damaged houses was a difficult exercise for them.
He said that most of the displaced families could not afford the reconstruction expenses while harsh cold weather was also a serious impediment in the reconstruction activities.

He also complained that the district administration delayed displaying the list of the approved returnees, leaving many to find out a day or two late. He suggested that names of the selected persons should be displayed at prominent places at least two days in advance of their return.
Published in Dawn, November 24th, 2026

text: QUETTA: The Balochistan government has announced rewards ranging from Rs500,000 to Rs250 million for providing authentic information about most-wanted terrorists in the province.

According to an official advertisement issued by the provincial government, a reward of Rs250m has been fixed for information about Bashir Zeb of the banned Balochistan Liberation Army and Abdul Rehman alias Rehman Gul.
Similar rewards have been fixed for other wanted persons depending on their status.
The government said the list has been issued as part of its efforts to maintain law and order and eliminate terrorism in the province.
Balochistan Home Affairs Adviser Babar Yousafzai affirmed that the provincial government was determined to eradicate terrorism and protect the lives and properties of citizens.
The list of most-wanted terrorists and the announcement of rewards were, therefore, part of the ongoing government measures against terrorism.
Yousafzai stressed that public cooperation was of utmost importance in the war against terrorism.
The adviser appealed to the public to contact the relevant institutions of the government if they had any authentic information regarding the wanted terrorists.

He said the identity of informants would be kept anonymous, and immediate action would be taken against the terrorists. Payment of rewards would be made according to the rules and regulations fixed by the government.

Pakistan has seen a surge in terrorism, especially in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan, since the banned Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan ended its ceasefire deal with the government in November 2022, vowing to increase attacks.

While Pakistan recorded fewer militant attacks from Nov 6 to 12, fatalities and injuries increased sharply, “highlighting the changing intensity and continued volatility of militant threat across the country”, according to the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies .
Balochistan recorded 13 attacks, resulting in eight deaths and 19 injuries, while KP “remained the principal centre of violence” with 16 attacks and 44 fatalities.
